title: Appointed times
hook: the second order: Shabbat, festivals and fasts

segments.voice: Yesterday, the corner of the field, and your line: the corner. Did you leave something where someone could take it without asking? Today, the second order, and the end of the week. Day one thousand seventy-one.

Two great sages disagree about when the new month began. It sounds small. It isn't. If the month started on a different day, then Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, falls on a different day too. Rabban Gamaliel, head of the court, has fixed the date. Rabbi Joshua is convinced he got it wrong. So Rabban Gamaliel sends him an order: come to me with your walking staff and your money, on the day that by your count is Yom Kippur. On a fast day, you don't travel or carry money. He is asking Rabbi Joshua to break his own holy day in public. What will he do? That's in the second order of the Mishnah.
screen: `WHEN DID THE MONTH BEGIN?` → `COME WITH YOUR STAFF AND YOUR MONEY.` → `ON YOUR OWN YOM KIPPUR.`

segments.voice: Moed. Appointed time. The second of the six orders is the order of holy time. Inside it are tractates named for the days themselves: Shabbat. Pesachim, for Passover. Yoma, the Day, meaning Yom Kippur. Sukkah. Rosh Hashanah. Taanit, on fasts. Megillah, on Purim. Over the coming days we'll open several of them. The name comes from the Torah's own words for the festivals. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "These are the appointed seasons of the LORD." And the verse goes on: holy gatherings, which ye shall proclaim. Now back to Rabbi Joshua, in tractate Rosh Hashanah. He is deeply troubled. Rabbi Akiva comes to him with that same verse. The festivals, Akiva says, are the ones you proclaim. Whether the court sets the date at the right time or not, these are the appointed seasons. Another sage adds: if we question every court's ruling, there will be no end to it. So Rabbi Joshua takes his staff and his money and walks to Rabban Gamaliel on the day he himself believed was Yom Kippur. And Rabban Gamaliel stands up, kisses him on the head, and says, in paraphrase: come in peace, my teacher and my student. My teacher in wisdom, my student because you accepted my word. That's what this order is about. Holy time has rules, and the rules are kept together. Now look back at the week. The tannaim and the amoraim, the teachers and the explainers. Shas, six orders. Seeds, blessings first, the corner. And today, the calendar a whole people keeps as one.
screen: `MOED: THE ORDER OF HOLY TIME.` · `THE APPOINTED SEASONS, WHICH YE PROCLAIM.` · `RABBI JOSHUA TAKES UP HIS STAFF.` · `MY TEACHER AND MY STUDENT.` · then, large: `HOLY TIME HAS RULES.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: look at the month ahead. Open your calendar, or picture it, and sit with it through the bell. Look for the times that are already appointed: a Shabbat, a holiday, a birthday, an anniversary of a loss, a standing dinner with someone you love. Notice which ones you protect and which ones get pushed around. Then choose one time in the coming month and decide to keep it, with the same steadiness a community keeps its calendar. If you keep Shabbat or the festivals, you might look at how this month's fall. The bell holds the time.
Moed. Appointed time: the second order of the Mishnah, on Shabbat, festivals and fasts, a calendar kept together. Today's word.
Your line: holy time has rules. Today, keep one appointment exactly as you promised, on time, without moving it. Tomorrow, the thirty-nine kinds of work. Day one thousand seventy-one.

howItsDone: Jews keep a shared calendar of Shabbat, festivals and fasts, and the laws for each are studied in the tractates of the order Moed; today the Hebrew calendar is fixed by calculation rather than by witnesses to the new moon.

notes: Week close (days 1065–1071): tannaim, amoraim, Shas, Zeraim, blessings first, peah, Moed.

Leviticus 23:4 quoted from JPS 1917 ('These are the appointed seasons of the LORD'); the rest of the verse ('holy convocations, which ye shall proclaim') is paraphrased as 'holy gatherings, which ye shall proclaim'. Please confirm the JPS 1917 wording.

Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 2:8–9 paraphrased: Rabban Gamaliel's ruling on the new moon; Rabbi Joshua's dissent; the order to come with staff and money on his Yom Kippur; Rabbi Akiva's reading of Leviticus 23:4; Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas's argument (given as 'another sage': if we question every court, there will be no end); Gamaliel's greeting 'my teacher and my student'. Please confirm.

Tractates named are a selection of Moed (Eruvin, Shekalim, Beitzah, Moed Katan and Chagigah not named); no count given. Later days (1072–1075) teach Shabbat's labors, the eruv, seder and sukkah, and Megillah/Taanit, so this day only names them.
howItsDone: 'the Hebrew calendar is fixed by calculation rather than by witnesses' is stated without a date; please confirm phrasing.
